headline.quick: 5 quick AWS questions on VPC DNS: base+2, private zones, Resolver endpoints
headline.dungeon: DNS war-game: zone associated, name not found; trace a tool loop; 10-q TD quiz

intel.title: Private hosted zones only answer through the VPC's own DNS
bullets: Every VPC has an Amazon-provided DNS server at the VPC CIDR base plus two: 10.20.0.2 for 10.20.0.0/16.
Private hosted zones need two VPC attributes set to true: enableDnsHostnames and enableDnsSupport.
If your instances use custom DNS servers, those servers must forward queries for the private zone to the Amazon-provided DNS server. Associating the zone with the VPC is not enough on its own.
Debug by asking both servers directly: dig @<custom server> name, then dig @<base+2> name. Different answers tell you which hop is missing.

source.title: Amazon Route 53 Developer Guide: Considerations when working with a private hosted zone

intel.why: Customers moving DNS to their own servers is one of the most common ways a working AWS deployment loses its private names overnight, and it is tonight's war-game.

question.q: EC2 instances in a VPC use custom DNS servers (set in the DHCP option set). A private hosted zone associated with that VPC returns NXDOMAIN. What must the custom DNS servers do, and which two VPC attributes must be true?
question.a: Forward queries for the private zone to the Amazon-provided DNS server at the VPC CIDR base plus two (10.20.0.2 for 10.20.0.0/16). enableDnsHostnames and enableDnsSupport must both be true.

quests.title: Micro-drill: 5 questions on VPC DNS
quests.brief: Original questions, no lookups. One line per answer. They set up tonight's DNS war-game.
tasks: Q1. A VPC uses 10.20.0.0/16. At which IPv4 address inside the VPC CIDR is the Amazon-provided DNS server (Route 53 Resolver)?
Q2. A private hosted zone is associated with a VPC, but nothing in the VPC can resolve its records. The DHCP option set is the default. Which two VPC attributes do you check first?

Q3. Servers in an on-premises data centre, connected over Site-to-Site VPN, must resolve names in a private hosted zone. Which Route 53 Resolver component do you create in the VPC, and what do the on-prem DNS servers point at it?
Q4. EC2 instances must resolve names in an on-prem domain (corp.example) that only the on-prem DNS servers know. Which two Route 53 Resolver pieces do you create?

Q5. api.example.com exists in a public hosted zone (203.0.113.10) and in a private hosted zone associated with your VPC (10.20.3.15). An instance in that VPC using Amazon DNS looks it up. Which address does it get?
quests.done_condition: You wrote 5 one-line answers and at least 4 match the answer key.
answer_key: Q1. 10.20.0.2: the VPC CIDR base plus two. (169.254.169.253 also reaches it, but it is not in the VPC CIDR.)
Q2. enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames. Both must be true for private hosted zones.
Q3. An inbound endpoint. The on-prem servers get a conditional forwarder for the private zone's domain that points at the inbound endpoint's IP addresses.
Q4. An outbound endpoint plus a forwarding rule for corp.example (targeting the on-prem DNS server IPs), associated with the VPC.
Q5. 10.20.3.15. Inside an associated VPC, the private hosted zone answers for its namespace, so the private record wins.

quests.title: War-Game 3: the zone is associated, the name does not exist
quests.brief: A customer changed their VPC's DNS servers to their AD domain controllers yesterday. Today the agent cannot reach its database and they want you to hard-code the IP. Set a 20-minute timer. Evidence is in the code block. Today's intel card helps.
quests.code:
# Customer: agent runs on EC2 (Ubuntu 24.04) in a VPC, CIDR 10.20.0.0/16.
#           Postgres for the agent is in the same VPC. Two AD domain controllers
#           run on EC2 in the VPC at 10.20.1.10 and 10.20.2.10.
# Quote: "Yesterday we pointed the VPC at our domain controllers so new boxes can join AD.
#         This morning the agent can't find its database. Route 53 must be broken,
#         the zone is right there and it's associated. Can you hard-code the IP?"

$ journalctl -u agent --since 06:00 --no-pager | tail -2
Nov 29 06:02:11 ip-10-20-4-23 agent[2211]: ERROR db connect failed: could not translate host name "db.aws.corp.example" to address: Name or service not known
Nov 29 06:02:13 ip-10-20-4-23 agent[2211]: ERROR retrying db connect (attempt 4/10)

$ getent hosts db.aws.corp.example; echo "exit=$?"
exit=2

$ nc -zv -w 3 10.20.3.41 5432
Connection to 10.20.3.41 5432 port [tcp/postgresql] succeeded!

$ resolvectl status ens5 | grep -E 'DNS Servers|DNS Domain'
       DNS Servers: 10.20.1.10 10.20.2.10
        DNS Domain: corp.example

$ aws ec2 describe-dhcp-options --dhcp-options-ids dopt-0c3e5f7a9b1d2e4f6 \
    --query 'DhcpOptions[0].DhcpConfigurations'
[
    {"Key": "domain-name", "Values": [{"Value": "corp.example"}]},
    {"Key": "domain-name-servers", "Values": [{"Value": "10.20.1.10"}, {"Value": "10.20.2.10"}]}
]

$ aws route53 list-hosted-zones-by-vpc --vpc-id vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718 \
    --vpc-region ap-southeast-2 --query 'HostedZoneSummaries[].Name'
[
    "aws.corp.example."
]

$ aws ec2 describe-vpc-attribute --vpc-id vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718 --attribute enableDnsSupport \
    --query 'EnableDnsSupport.Value'
true

$ dig @10.20.1.10 db.aws.corp.example +noall +comments +authority   # trimmed
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NXDOMAIN, id: 50314
;; flags: qr aa rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 0, AUTHORITY: 1, ADDITIONAL: 1
;; AUTHORITY SECTION:
corp.example.		3600	IN	SOA	dc01.corp.example. hostmaster.corp.example. 4123 900 600 86400 3600
tasks: Sort the evidence: which lines prove the network path is fine, and which prove the failure is name resolution?
Name the server that answered NXDOMAIN and explain, from the SOA line, why it answered with authority.
Write the 4-bullet RCA brief, one line each: [C] confirmed signal (facts only), [I] root-cause hypothesis, [?] the single highest-value verification command, [Fix] the minimal reversible remediation.
One line: why hard-coding 10.20.3.41 in the agent config is the wrong fix.
quests.done_condition: Four RCA bullets are written, [C] holds only facts from the evidence, [?] is one command, and [Fix] keeps AD join working.
answer_key: Network is fine: nc to 10.20.3.41:5432 succeeds. Resolution is the failure: libpq 'could not translate host name', and getent exit 2 (key not found).

dc01 (10.20.1.10) answered NXDOMAIN with the aa flag because it is authoritative for corp.example (the SOA in the authority section). aws.corp.example is a subdomain it does not delegate or forward, so it says the name does not exist.

[C] Since the DHCP option set change, the instance resolves through 10.20.1.10/10.20.2.10. The DC answers NXDOMAIN, authoritatively, for db.aws.corp.example. The private hosted zone aws.corp.example is associated with the VPC and enableDnsSupport is true. The database is reachable by IP.

[I] Private hosted zone records are answered by the Amazon-provided DNS server (VPC base + 2 = 10.20.0.2). The DCs are now the instances' resolvers and do not forward aws.corp.example there, so the private zone is never consulted.

[?] dig @10.20.0.2 db.aws.corp.example +short from the agent host. An answer of 10.20.3.41 confirms the zone is fine and the forwarding path is missing. (Also confirm enableDnsHostnames is true; the evidence only shows enableDnsSupport.)

[Fix] On the DCs, add a conditional forwarder for aws.corp.example pointing at 10.20.0.2, which is what the Route 53 docs require for custom DNS servers. It keeps AD join working and is reversible by deleting the forwarder. Reverting the DHCP option set also fixes the agent but breaks the customer's AD join.
Hard-coding the IP hides the defect: every other private-zone name in the VPC is broken too, and the IP silently goes stale on the next database failover or replacement.
Bonus smell: the agent retries a resolution failure 10 times. NXDOMAIN from an authoritative server will not fix itself in seconds.

quests.title: Trace tool dispatch and the stop condition
quests.brief: A scripted fake call_model replays five replies: good tool call, bad arguments, unknown tool, good call, final answer. Trace run() by hand and predict every line before you run it. AI autocomplete off, docs allowed.
tasks: Keep a table for the first run(): turn, the reply, which branch runs (final / unknown tool / TypeError / success), and what is appended to messages.
Write the exact output of the whole program (10 lines).
Explain in one line why the second run() replays the same replies from the start, unlike yesterday's mutable-default call_model.
Predict what happens if the third reply is changed to '{"tool": "add", "argz": {"q": "dns"}}'. Name the exception and the line that raises it.
Name the line that is the stop condition and the line that is the turn cap. One sentence: which one would catch a model that never says final?
Save it as trace03.py, run python3 trace03.py; echo $?, and compare with your table.
quests.done_condition: Your written 10-line output matches the real run exactly and the exit code is 0.
answer_key: Real output (Python 3.13, exit code 0), run 1: '1 get_weather -> {'city': 'Perth', 'temp_c': 31}' / '2 add -> {'error': "add() got an unexpected keyword argument 'c'"}' / '3 search -> {'error': 'unknown tool search'}' / '4 add -> 5' / 'stopped: turn cap 4'.
Run 2 (max_turns=5): the same four tool lines again, then 'done in 5: Perth is 31C and 2 + 3 = 5'.
Bad args and unknown tools do not crash the loop: they become error results appended as a tool message, so the model can correct itself. That is the pattern the raid boss needs.
call_model picks the reply by counting assistant messages, and each run() starts with a fresh messages list, so the count restarts at 0. No hidden state survives between calls.

With 'argz' (run, exit code 1): turns 1 and 2 print as before, then reply['args'] raises KeyError: 'args' on the line result = fn(**reply['args']). It is outside the try, and the try only catches TypeError, so the program crashes. Tool-arg validation is Day 8's fill-in.
Stop condition: if "final" in reply. Turn cap: for turn in range(1, max_turns + 1) and the return after the loop. Only the turn cap catches a model that never says final.
Note: with max_turns=4 the final answer is never read, even though the model would have given it on turn 5. A cap that is too tight looks like a failed agent.
